title: Ontario Calls in Police as College Recruitment Pipeline Under Scrutiny
excerpt: Ontario has referred suspected criminal misuse of student financial aid at private career colleges to provincial police, after inspectors linked student accounts and $219 million in public funds to a network of immigration recruitment firms.
body:
• Ontario has referred suspected criminal misuse of student financial aid at private career colleges to the Ontario Provincial Police.
  • Inspectors allege third parties completed coursework for students, with 39 of 42 files at one Toronto campus sharing login activity tied to a single recruiter.
  • What this means for you: before signing with any Canadian college or agent, verify the school's current registration and OSAP eligibility on Ontario's official career-college registry, keep every receipt and contract, and never let an agent control your login credentials or application portal.
  • The three flagship campuses involved received more than $219 million in OSAP grants for about 14,800 students in 2024-25 — over half of what every public college in the province received combined.

Ontario has asked the Ontario Provincial Police to investigate suspected criminal misuse of public student-aid money at private career colleges, the provincial government said this week, after auditors found what they called "serious concerns" about enrolment fraud, third parties completing coursework, and colleges closely linked to immigration recruitment firms.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn said the ministry launched targeted inspections last year, then hired KPMG in August to audit student-assistance payments. Preliminary findings included common ownership between colleges and immigration services firms, co-location of recruitment agencies with college campuses, weak student identity verification, and unusual concentrations of financial-aid applications from the same geographic locations.

The inspection trail

The details come from court records filed as three Academy of Learning locations — Bay Street in downtown Toronto, Brampton East and North York — fight the province's decision to strip them of OSAP eligibility, according to reporting by The Canadian Press. At the Bay Street campus, 39 of 42 student files examined by inspectors had IP addresses also used to access other students' accounts — and every one of those students had been referred by the same recruiter. One Brampton student's account showed all quizzes and the final exam for a business course completed on the same day, the exam itself taking six minutes. Another submitted a final exam on the first day they ever opened the course.

https://x.com/TheTorontoSun/status/2107630771666129205

Inspectors who reached six students by phone found some unable to name their institution, programme or courses. Federal regulators had separately flagged the Bay and Brampton locations in September 2025, and Career Colleges Ontario warned in February 2026 that some schools used agents promising to redirect students to institutions that would falsely report attendance.

"This pattern suggests shared login credentials, unauthorized access, and/or co-ordinated activity among users."

— Ontario ministry inspection report, quoted in court records

Context and background

The recruitment pipeline at the centre of this scandal is the same machine that has fed hundreds of thousands of Indian students into Canadian colleges. Education agents in India — numbering in the thousands, with roughly 1,700 in Gujarat alone according to India's Enforcement Directorate — recruit students on commission. The ED has said about 112 Canadian colleges held agreements with one Mumbai-based entity and more than 150 with another, referring some 35,000 students a year between them, and is probing whether colleges near the Canada-U.S. border were used to traffic Indian nationals.

Impact and analysis

The scale of public money is striking. Freedom-of-information data obtained by The Canadian Press shows the three Academy of Learning locations collected more than $219 million in OSAP grants for about 14,800 students in 2024-25, while every publicly funded college in Ontario received about $385 million. Aid applications at the flagged schools grew an estimated 500 to 600 per cent over two years.

On May 1, Quinn notified five career colleges that their students would lose OSAP eligibility effective August 1, 2026. The schools are challenging the decision in court; the Academy of Learning denies most allegations, attributes some findings to dynamic IP addresses, and says it has added two-factor authentication and tighter identity checks. None of the allegations has been proven in court.

The diaspora angle

India is Canada's largest source of international students — roughly 427,000 were enrolled in 2024 — and the recruitment pipeline under scrutiny is overwhelmingly an India-facing business: agents collecting lakhs per student, with families mortgaging land to fund the journey. When a college loses aid eligibility, the students holding the receipt are usually the ones with the least cushion. Treat recruitment agents as financial intermediaries, not trusted advisers, and verify everything independently.

What's next

The OPP will now decide whether the audit findings merit a criminal investigation. Separately, the judicial review of the OSAP-eligibility decision will set a precedent for how aggressively Ontario can regulate the sector. For students already enrolled at affected campuses, regulators' advice is blunt: check your OSAP account directly, keep every document, and confirm in writing what happens to your funding if your school's status changes.
